summary:
HydroGeoPulse uses NASA’s GRACE satellites, which “weigh” how much water a region holds, from space, to spot whether a place is gaining or losing water over 24 years, and to prove the change is real rather than random noise.

Most tools over-claim: on realistic data, the standard test wrongly “finds” a trend 41% of the time. HydroGeoPulse corrects this and cuts false alarms to about 19% — and we proved it by testing our methods on data where we already knew the right answer.

Across eight regions it found three major farming areas losing groundwater (northern India, northern China, California), East Africa’s lakes gaining water, and four “control” regions correctly showing no change.

It has two modes: plain English for the public, and full technical detail for scientists. 

This matter is especially crucial as groundwater feeds billions of people, and because losing that water literally shifts the ground beneath us, with links to land sinking and even catastrophic earthquakes. We built an rigorously tested Earth-system detection, for everyone.
details:
What it does & how it works
HydroGeoPulse lets anyone pick a region of Earth and find out whether its water storage is genuinely rising, falling, or holding steady over the past ~24 years. And whether that change is statistically real or just noise. It uses NASA GRACE/GRACE-FO satellites, which detect tiny changes in Earth’s gravity to “weigh” how much water a region holds. The process: area-average the satellite water-storage grid over a chosen basin, remove the predictable yearly wet/dry cycle (harmonic regression), measure the long-term rate of change (Theil–Sen slope), test its significance with a Mann–Kendall test corrected for autocorrelation, and attach an honest confidence interval via block bootstrapping. It also flags unusually wet or dry months.

Benefits & intended impact
Groundwater sustains billions of people’s food and water, and its slow depletion is often invisible until a crisis hits. HydroGeoPulse surfaces these trends early and verifies they’re real, so decisions aren’t based on false signals. Because water mass physically loads Earth’s crust, the same trends connect to measurable ground motion, land subsidence, and even fault stress, linking hydrology to solid-Earth hazard such as earthquakes.

A plain-English mode makes it usable by students and the public (the challenge’s target audience), while a technical mode serves scientists.

How it’s creative
Most trend tools stop at “is there a trend?” HydroGeoPulse asks “can you trust it?” — and proves its own answer. We ran a Monte-Carlo “lie-detector”: on 500 synthetic series with no real trend, the standard test falsely reported one 41% of the time; our corrected method cut that to ~19%. We also benchmarked three anomaly detectors (2σ, MAD, Isolation Forest) against data with known anomalies and honestly chose the simplest robust method when the machine-learning option didn’t beat it, which shows we prioritise judgment over hype. The dual plain/technical interface and the hydrology-to-solid-Earth bridge are further original touches.

Tools & technology
Python; NASA JPL GRACE/GRACE-FO Mascon data (PO.DAAC / Earthdata); xarray + netCDF4 for the satellite grids; NumPy, pandas, SciPy, statsmodels, pymannkendall, and scikit-learn for statistics and anomaly detection; Matplotlib for figures; Streamlit + Plotly for the interactive app (including a 3-D globe); deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud. Open-source on GitHub.

Factors we considered
Scientific honesty above all — we report “no trend” where there is none, correct for the statistical traps that fool naive tools, and validate our methods against ground truth.

Accessibility — a high-schooler and a geophysicist should both understand it.

And scientific grounding — every claim about deeper Earth-system significance is backed by peer-reviewed research (Materna et al. 2021; Amos et al. 2014).
